definition.text: An economic system that tries to keep products, parts and materials in use at their highest value for as long as possible.

facts.text: It is set against the linear 'take-make-waste' economy, in which resources are extracted, used and thrown away, putting heavy pressure on the environment.
Extracting and processing material resources accounts for over 55 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Circularity can be raised in four ways: narrowing the loop (using fewer resources), slowing it (reuse and repair), closing it (recycling), and substituting renewable or less harmful inputs.
The European Parliament describes it as sharing, leasing, reusing, repairing, refurbishing and recycling existing materials and products for as long as possible.
Global implementation could cut emissions by 22.8 billion tons, equal to 39% of global emissions in 2019.
Kenneth Boulding's 1966 essay 'The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth' contrasted an open 'cowboy economy' with a closed one and is often cited as the idea's first expression.
Pearce and Turner's 1990 book described a system where waste from extraction, production and consumption is turned back into inputs.
The concept draws on industrial ecology, biomimicry and cradle-to-cradle design; the Ellen MacArthur Foundation spread it in Europe and the Americas.

title: R-hierarchies of circularity
article: Circular economy#"Re-" models to rank circularity priority

definition.text: Ranked lists of 're-' actions (refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle and so on) that order circular strategies by how much value they keep or waste they avoid.

facts.text: They are probably inspired by the 1970s motto 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle'.
In 2018 Reike and colleagues compared 69 different R hierarchies and found 38 distinct 're' words, which they unified into a 10R framework.
Refusing and reducing raw material use rank highest; reuse, repair, refurbishing, remanufacturing and repurposing come next; recycling and then energy recovery by incineration rank lowest.

title: Critiques of the circular economy
article: Circular economy#Critiques of circular economy models

definition.text: Objections that the circular economy keeps growth unquestioned, ignores economics and thermodynamics, and neglects social justice.

facts.text: Zink and Geyer argued proponents treat the world as an engineering system and questioned whether closing loops really prevents new primary production.
Because of the second law of thermodynamics, recovering dispersed materials takes energy that rises nonlinearly as recycled shares rise, so recovery can never be 100%.
Product-level efficiency gains can be offset by growth in total consumption, so some argue for a post-growth circular economy.
Most circular economy plans do not ask who controls the technologies or how costs and benefits are shared, prompting calls for a 'circular society'.

contested_note: Scholars dispute whether closing material loops actually displaces primary production and whether circularity is compatible with growth.

title: Circular business models

definition.text: Ways of running a firm, such as product-as-a-service, sharing platforms and life-extension services, that make money while keeping resources in use.

facts.text: They aim to use resources better, cut waste and create value for firms and customers.
A key idea is to create loops that recapture value that would otherwise be lost.
Firms adopting secondary raw materials do not necessarily cut short-term costs and may face higher perceived production costs.
Digital tools such as the internet of things, big data and AI are seen as key enablers for scaling them up.
Early talk of circularity centred on 're-X' steps such as recycling, remanufacturing, reuse and recovery.
Four strategies: narrowing loops (using fewer materials), slowing loops (repair, reuse, resale, rental), closing loops (recycling into new production) and regenerating natural systems.
They can cut costs and create new offers, but face hurdles in technology, consumer habits and profitability.

notes: The Circular economy page also has a 'Circular business models' section; it may duplicate an entry in the circular-and-bio-based-economies chapter.

definition.text: Formal standards that guide organisations in applying circular economy principles.

facts.text: In 2017 the British Standards Institution launched BS 8001:2017, the first circular economy standard.
ISO set up technical committee TC 323 in 2018 and in 2024 and 2025 published four ISO 59000-series standards, including ISO 59020 on measuring circularity performance.

title: EU Circular Economy Action Plan
article: Circular economy#Circular Economy Action Plan of 2020

definition.text: The European Union's policy programme for moving its economy toward circularity.

facts.text: The first plan, 'Closing the loop', had 54 measures aimed at competitiveness, growth and jobs.
The European Commission adopted the new plan in March 2020; it targets resource-intensive industries, waste reduction, decarbonisation and standard sustainable products.

title: Dematerialization

definition.text: Making more goods, or serving the same economic needs, with less material.

facts.text: It can be absolute or relative: a cut in total material use, or in material per unit of economic output.
Products are dematerialised in three ways: optimising (less mass), digitising (paper to e-book) and servitising (renting instead of selling).
Between 1977 and 2001 the material needed to meet Americans' needs fell from 1.18 to 1.08 trillion pounds while population grew by 55 million.
Cars weigh 30% less than in the early 1960s, and aluminium soda cans are six times lighter.
Critics note extraction of six minerals and cement production grew faster than GDP from 1960 to 2019.
Part of rich countries' dematerialisation comes from outsourcing material-intensive production to developing countries.

contested_note: Critics say there is little evidence of global dematerialization, only regional shifts caused by outsourcing.

definition.text: The study of how materials and energy flow through industrial systems.

facts.text: It aims to move industry from open-loop systems, where resources end as waste, to closed loops where wastes become inputs for new processes.
Its name reflects the idea of using natural ecosystems, which have no waste, as a model for designing sustainable industry.
Main research areas include industrial metabolism, life-cycle assessment, eco-design, extended producer responsibility and eco-industrial parks.
It was popularised in a 1989 Scientific American article by Robert Frosch and Nicholas Gallopoulos, who asked why one industry's outputs could not be another's inputs.
It combines engineering, economics, sociology, toxicology and the natural sciences.
Its principles are now appearing in policy areas such as the circular economy, for example by using waste heat from one process to run a cooler one.

title: Bioeconomy

definition.text: The part of the economy that uses renewable biological resources and biotechnology to produce food, materials, products and energy.

facts.text: Its resources come from land and sea: crops, forests, fish, animals and micro-organisms.
It aims to secure food, use natural resources more sustainably and reduce dependence on fossil resources and minerals.
The term became popular from the mid-2000s when the EU and OECD adopted it as a policy framework; the OECD (2006) and EU (2012) created bioeconomy strategies.
Its products include food, feed, bio-based products, bioenergy and services based on biological resources.
Critics fear its 'green growth' framing keeps an unsustainable model in place and may lead to an economisation of living things.

contested_note: Some argue the bioeconomy's green-growth vision sustains rather than changes an unsustainable economic model.

definition.text: A bioeconomy run on circular principles, producing food, materials and energy from renewable biological resources while reducing dependence on natural resources.

facts.text: According to the European Commission's science service it produces €1.5 trillion in value added, 11% of EU GDP.
One study found a circular bioeconomy may be necessary for a carbon-neutral future in line with the Paris Agreement.

title: Cascading use of biomass
article: Bioeconomy#Getting the most out of the biomass

definition.text: Processing biomass in an ordered pattern so that it yields the highest-value products before lower-value ones.

facts.text: The order runs from fine chemicals and medicines, through chemicals and bioplastics and transport fuels, to electricity and heat, which need the most biomass for the least value.
Finding the best pattern for a given biomass is called biorefining.

definition.text: A family of plastics made from biological rather than fossil sources, with different properties and uses.

facts.text: Some bioplastics are made from sugar by genetically modified microbes.
Biodegradable plastic has been made from chicken feathers, which are 90% keratin and over 6 million tons of waste a year in the EU and US.

definition.text: A nature-inspired way of designing products and systems in which materials are treated as nutrients that circulate safely and endlessly.

facts.text: The name plays on the phrase 'cradle to grave', the usual one-way path of a product from making to disposal.
It aims for systems that are not only efficient but essentially waste-free.
It builds on John T. Lyle's regenerative design and can be applied to cities, buildings, economies and social systems as well as products.
At Ford's River Rouge plant, a planted roof formed part of an $18 million rainwater system that saved Ford $30 million in mechanical treatment facilities.
Recycling sites usually crush whole products rather than taking them apart, which makes recovering rare-earth elements and sorting alloys uneconomical.
'Cradle to Cradle' is a trademark of the consultancy MBDC, which in 2012 handed its certification to an independent non-profit institute after criticism.

definition.text: The cradle-to-cradle split of all materials into technical nutrients, which cycle in industry, and biological nutrients, which return safely to nature.

facts.text: Technical nutrients are non-toxic synthetic materials such as plastics and metals that can be used again and again without losing quality.
Biological nutrients are organic materials that decompose into soil and feed small life forms without harming the environment.
In a hypothetical cradle-to-cradle shoe, the sole is a biological nutrient and the upper a technical one, separated when the shoe is returned.

definition.text: Reusing materials to make products of lower quality or value than the original.

facts.text: A plastic computer case might become a plastic cup and then a park bench, ending eventually as plastic waste.
Cradle-to-cradle design aims to keep technical materials cycling at full quality instead of being downcycled.

definition.text: A product certification run by the Cradle to Cradle Products Innovation Institute that scores products against cradle-to-cradle criteria.

facts.text: Its criteria include material health, which identifies the chemicals in a product, and material reutilization, which covers recovery and recycling at end of life.
Materials are ranked green (low risk), yellow (acceptable), red (to be phased out) or grey (incomplete data).

definition.text: A part of industrial ecology in which separate firms exchange materials, energy, water and by-products so that one firm's waste becomes another's input.

facts.text: Such networks optimise material and energy use beyond what any single process could achieve alone.
Collaboration and geographic proximity are seen as its keys, though proximity is neither necessary nor sufficient.
At Kalundborg in Denmark, a power station's gypsum by-product becomes raw material for a plasterboard maker.
The Kalundborg web of exchanges evolved spontaneously over a long time; designing such systems from above in a short time is hard.
By-products are usually treated as waste and not listed on any exchange, so information about them is hard to get.
Keeping resources in use longer reduces demands on Earth's resources and is a stepping-stone toward a circular economy.

definition.text: A group of businesses on shared land that work together on environmental and resource issues to improve their environmental, economic and social performance.

facts.text: Firms in such parks physically exchange materials, energy, water and by-products, a form of industrial symbiosis.
They may share waste treatment, move by-products between plants, and reuse one plant's processed water in another.

definition.text: A method for measuring the flows and stocks of materials or substances within a clearly defined system.

facts.text: It is a core method of industrial ecology and of the study of social and industrial metabolism.
It rests on two principles: a systems approach and mass balance, the conservation of matter.
Every MFA system has a boundary, processes, flows between processes and stocks within them.
Unlike economic accounting, it also covers waste flows, emissions and natural resources that have no market.
It can be applied to a single plant, a supply chain, a product's life cycle, or a whole national economy.
The method was developed during the 1980s and 1990s.

definition.text: A ranking of ways to deal with waste, from the most to the least environmentally preferable, usually drawn as a pyramid.

facts.text: Its aim is to get the most practical benefit from products while generating the least waste.
The EU's 2008 Waste Framework Directive sets five steps in order: prevention, reuse, recycling, other recovery including energy recovery, and safe disposal as a last resort.
The idea traces to 'Lansink's Ladder', proposed by Dutch MP Ad Lansink in 1979.
Applied well, it can cut greenhouse gas emissions and pollutants, save energy and resources, create jobs and spur green technology.
Life-cycle thinking can justify departing from it: replacing an old, inefficient washing machine is often better than keeping it, because most of its impact comes during use.
An early EU proposal that put recycling level with incineration was heavily criticised and replaced by the five-step version.

definition.text: Cutting hazardous and other waste before it arises, by changing how things are produced.

facts.text: It works through changes in manufacturing technology, raw materials and product formulation, and is sometimes called pollution prevention.
Toxics use reduction, a more controversial form, targets upstream use of toxic chemicals and has been opposed by chemical manufacturers.

definition.text: Applying the circular economy to clothing so that fashion products last longer and are reused, recycled or repurposed instead of discarded.

facts.text: It replaces the take-make-use-dispose model with reduce, reuse, recycle and regenerate.
Practices include designing clothes for longevity, sustainable materials, recycling programmes and second-hand markets.
A 2017 Ellen MacArthur Foundation report, 'A New Textiles Economy', brought the term into the mainstream.

definition.text: Buying goods and services that follow circular economy principles, favouring reuse, durability and recycling to extend product lives and cut waste.

facts.text: It may mean buying durable or reusable goods, shared-use models, refurbished assets or products with recycled content.
It is often seen as part of sustainable procurement and supports SDG 12's target on sustainable public procurement.
Risks include greenwashing, and barriers include high infrastructure costs and no standard definitions.

definition.text: A facility that converts biomass into energy and other useful products such as chemicals.

facts.text: The IEA defines biorefining as sustainable processing of biomass into food, feed, chemicals, materials and bioenergy.
Like an oil refinery, it splits biomass into intermediates such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats; each refining step is called a cascading phase.
Its goals include supplying fuels and chemicals, creating rural jobs, valorising waste and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
Systems are classified by platform, product, feedstock and conversion process (mechanical, biochemical, chemical or thermochemical).
Biobased products can still cause land-use change, eutrophication and pesticide pollution, so life cycle assessment is used to compare them with conventional options.
The pulp and paper industry is considered the first industrialised biorefinery system.

title: Eco-efficiency

definition.text: Providing goods and services that meet human needs while steadily cutting their environmental impact and resource use over their whole life cycle.

facts.text: It means creating more goods and services with fewer resources and less waste and pollution.
It is measured as the ratio of value produced, such as GDP, to environmental impact, such as CO2 emissions.
The World Business Council for Sustainable Development coined the term in its 1992 publication 'Changing Course', and the 1992 Earth Summit endorsed it.
With consistency and eco-sufficiency, it is one of the three basic sustainability strategies.
It relies on technological innovation, business, markets, and an acceptance of growth.
Huesemann and Huesemann showed with historical evidence that efficiency gains have not reduced overall resource use and pollution.

contested_note: Critics argue efficiency gains alone have not reduced total resource use and pollution.

definition.text: An approach that looks at and reduces a product's environmental impacts at every stage of its life, from raw materials to disposal.

facts.text: A core aim is to avoid burden shifting, where an improvement at one stage causes harm at another.
Companies use it to design greener products, consumers to choose products, and governments to write regulations.
Its tools include life-cycle assessment, life cycle management, life cycle costing, design for the environment, product-service systems and integrated product policy.
Life-cycle assessment looks at impacts from raw material extraction through manufacture, distribution, use, repair, disposal and recycling.
The EU Waste Framework Directive brought life-cycle thinking into waste policy.

definition.text: Adding up all the costs a product or system incurs over its whole life to find the cheapest way of providing it.

facts.text: Product-service systems use it by lowering the maintenance and storage costs a consumer would otherwise bear.
Life cycle thinking shows how the environmental cost of owning a product depends on its running costs for energy and consumables.

definition.text: A policy approach that reduces product-related environmental damage by acting at whichever life-cycle stage is most effective.

facts.text: It combines economic instruments, substance bans, voluntary agreements, eco-labels and design guidelines rather than one measure.
The European Commission issued a green paper on it on 7 February 2001.

definition.text: Charging households for rubbish collection according to how much waste they put out, instead of a flat fee.

facts.text: Under a flat rate or tax, everyone pays the same and there is no incentive to reduce waste.
It rests on the polluter pays principle and shared responsibility.
Waste can be measured by weight, size, or counts of special bags, tags or containers; recycling and composting are often collected free.
In North America it cut residential waste by 9-38% and raised recycling by 6-40%.
In Ferrara, Italy, it led to a 30% overall drop in waste and a 40% rise in recycling.
Charging for waste can lead to illegal dumping ('fly-tipping').

definition.text: The build-up in the environment of plastic objects and particles, such as bottles, bags and microbeads, that harms people, wildlife and habitats.

facts.text: Plastics are cheap and durable, so manufacturers favour them, but most resist natural breakdown and degrade slowly.
Pollutant plastics are sorted by size into micro-, meso- and macro-debris; macrodebris is larger than 20 mm.
Around 275 million tonnes of plastic waste is generated each year, of which between 4.8 and 12.7 million tonnes is dumped into the sea.
Packaging is the largest use of plastic, at 219 Mt as of 2024.
More than 900 marine species are affected by plastic pollution.
Governments most often target plastic bags, by bans or fees, followed by plastic cutlery and microbeads.
Industry leaders knew in the early 1970s that most plastic would never be recycled, yet later ran a $50 million a year campaign saying it was.
Many academics and NGOs call for a legally binding international treaty that would cap plastic production.

definition.text: Tiny insoluble plastic particles, from 1 micrometre to 5 mm across, that pollute water, soil and air.

facts.text: Primary microplastics, such as microbeads, clothing microfibres and pellets, are already small when released; secondary ones come from larger items breaking down.
By 2050 the weight of microplastics in the sea is estimated to exceed that of fish.
Because some plastics take hundreds to thousands of years to degrade, microplastics are likely to be eaten and accumulate in organisms.

definition.text: An approach in which everyone who makes, sells, buys, uses or disposes of a product shares responsibility for reducing its environmental and health impacts over its life.

facts.text: For manufacturers it includes planning, and if necessary paying, for recycling or disposal at end of life.
Products can be redesigned to use fewer harmful substances and be more durable, reusable and recyclable.
It differs from extended producer responsibility, which places the burden on manufacturers, by spreading it to retailers, consumers and recyclers too.
Australia's Product Stewardship Act 2011 created voluntary, co-regulatory and mandatory schemes; its TV and computer scheme has recycled about 230,000 tonnes of e-waste.

definition.text: A system in which buyers pay a refundable fee on a bottle or container, which they get back when they return it.

facts.text: Unclaimed fees can pay for landfill or litter control.
Anyone who finds and returns a bottle can claim the fee, so collecting them is a means of survival for some homeless people in US cities.
The same principle is applied to paint and tyres, where buyers pay up front for disposing of the toxic waste they become.

definition.text: A business model in which a firm sells a combined package of products and services that together meet a customer's need.

facts.text: The idea is that customers want the function a product provides, not necessarily to own it, so firms may be paid per unit of service delivered.

Research identifies three classes: product-oriented (ownership passes with added services), use-oriented (the provider keeps ownership and sells use through sharing, pooling or leasing) and result-oriented (services replace products).
Examples include Xerox's pay-per-copy model and Philips' pay-per-lux lighting, where customers pay for a promised level of light.
Not every PSS reduces material use, but they are increasingly seen as part of firms' environmental strategy.
The concept was first developed at the Politecnico di Milano between 1993 and 1996.
Some authors claim PSS can improve eco-efficiency by a factor of 4 or more.

definition.text: Meeting customer needs by selling a product's function or output, or a product-service package, rather than the product itself.

facts.text: It turns a one-time sale into a long-term service relationship, such as a maintenance-free service contract.
It can give access to people who cannot afford to buy outright, as with car-pooling, car-sharing or rent-to-own.
Servitizing, alongside optimizing and digitizing, is one of three main ways to dematerialize a product.

definition.text: Turning waste materials into new materials and objects.

facts.text: It is the third step in the 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' hierarchy.
It saves materials and energy and reduces greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution from incineration and water pollution from landfills.
Ideally a material becomes a fresh supply of the same material, as metal cans can; for many materials that is hard or costly, so they become different, lesser products.
Recycling aluminium uses only 5% of the energy of virgin production.
Two-thirds of all new steel is estimated to come from recycled steel.
Much of the difficulty comes from products not being designed for recycling; in the USA only about 6 to 7 percent of plastic is recycled.
Large investment in recycling came in the 1970s because of rising energy costs.

definition.text: The main ways of recycling, grouped by process and by what the material becomes.

facts.text: Mechanical recycling shreds, melts and reforms materials, while chemical recycling breaks them into chemical components.
Closed-loop recycling makes the same product without significant quality loss; open-loop recycling makes different, often lower-quality products.
Closed-loop recycling is generally seen as more sustainable because it loses fewer resources.

title: Economics of recycling

definition.text: The dispute over whether recycling's economic and environmental benefits outweigh its costs.

facts.text: Critics argue collection and transport costs and energy can outweigh the savings in production.
It is often cheaper for cities to landfill household waste than to recycle it, and virgin plastic resin costs 40 percent less than recycled resin.
Comparing only market prices ignores externalities, such as the extra pollution from making new plastic.
Life cycle assessment can measure these externalities, and tools such as a carbon tax can bring them into market prices.
Communities save money when recycling replaces, rather than adds to, their usual waste system.

contested_note: Critics and proponents disagree over whether recycling's costs and energy use exceed its savings.

definition.text: The ways recyclables are gathered from the waste stream: drop-off centres, buy-back centres and curbside collection.

facts.text: Systems trade off public convenience against government ease and expense.
Buy-back centres pay for cleaned, sorted recyclables, giving a clear incentive; drop-off centres are easiest to set up but have low, unpredictable throughput.
Source separation, where each material is sorted before collection, gives the purest recyclates.

definition.text: Laws that secure a steady supply of recyclable material and a market for recycled products.

facts.text: Supply is created by mandatory collection, container deposit laws and refuse bans.
Demand is raised by minimum recycled content mandates, utilization rates, procurement policies and recycled-product labelling.

definition.text: Rebuilding a used product to the original maker's specifications from a mix of reused, repaired and new parts.

facts.text: Unlike other recovery processes, it is complete: a remanufactured machine should meet the same customer expectations as a new one.
A discarded product is fully taken apart, usable parts are cleaned and refurbished, and it is reassembled into a unit equal or sometimes better than new.
In 2020 it made up 2% of all US manufacturing and 1.9% in the EU.
It can be done with or without loss of the original product's identity, as with photocopiers and toner cartridges.

definition.text: Using wastes as raw material to make valuable new products.

facts.text: It aims to cut waste and landfill needs while getting the most value from waste, and it delays the need for raw materials.
It is part of a circular economy that minimises resource extraction and waste.
Metals such as lithium, cobalt and vanadium can be recovered from industrial landfills and old mine wastes for electric vehicles and wind turbines.
Its potential shrinks because materials are irreversibly mixed and diluted (their entropy rises) through manufacture, use and landfilling.
Capturing landfill gas for energy counts as recovery but is a last resort, since the point is to avoid landfill altogether.

definition.text: Recovering water, energy, nutrients and other materials from wastewater, sewage sludge and human excreta.

facts.text: Sewage systems were first designed only to carry waste away; since the 1970s the focus moved to cleaning water, and since about 2003 to recovering resources.
Nutrients in wastewater and excreta are widely reused in farming, often unsafely; WHO guidelines from 2006 set a framework for doing it safely.

definition.text: Biological processes that break down organic waste such as food scraps and garden material into compost, fertiliser and energy.

facts.text: Methane from digestion can be captured to generate electricity and heat.
Anaerobic digestion of the organic part of municipal waste has been found more environmentally effective than landfill, incineration or pyrolysis.

definition.text: Using an item for a purpose other than the one it was made for, usually something considered junk.

facts.text: Examples include tyres used as boat fenders and drums used as feeding troughs or compost bins.
Earthship houses use tyres as insulating walls and bottles as glass walls.

definition.text: The legal right of owners to maintain, repair or modify their own devices and equipment, such as cars, electronics and farm machinery.

facts.text: Obstacles such as manufacturer-only servicing, restricted parts and tools, and software locks create a 'repair monopoly'.
Repair monopolies have been found to raise prices, cause delays and reduce consumer choice.
Its goals are to favour repair over replacement and make repairs cheaper, supporting a more sustainable economy and less electronic waste.
Broken and used electronics became the fastest-growing waste stream as smartphones and computers spread.
The EU adopted its Right to Repair Directive on 30 May 2024, and Canada became the first country with a national right-to-repair law on 7 November 2024.

title: Sharing economy

definition.text: An economic system in which people share in making, distributing, trading and using goods and services, often through online platforms.

facts.text: It puts the spare capacity of goods and services to use; the classic example is that the average car sits unused 95% of the time.
It can be run by non-profits, like a lending library, or by companies for profit, such as Uber and Airbnb.
It can reduce environmental harm by cutting the number of goods that must be produced.
There is no consensus on its definition.
Critics say platforms avoid taxes, regulation and insurance costs and can cause a 'race to the bottom' in wages.
Whether its workers should be treated as independent contractors or employees is debated.

contested_note: Its labour effects and whether its gains come from real efficiency or from avoiding regulation are disputed.

definition.text: A systemic approach to using and reusing materials more productively across their whole life cycle.

facts.text: Global raw material use rose during the 20th century at about twice the rate of population growth.
Each 1 percent rise in GDP has raised raw material use by 0.4 percent.
Unlike waste management, which deals only with end-of-life waste, it covers the whole life cycle and holds every industry and consumer in it responsible.
The OECD and the US EPA have adopted it; the OECD issued a policy brief on it in 2012.

definition.text: The conventional 'take-make-waste' economy in which resources are extracted, made into products, used and thrown away.

facts.text: Its processes use up finite reserves to make short-lived products that end in landfills or incinerators.
It puts great pressure on the environment through extraction, energy-intensive production and large amounts of waste.
The circular economy and circular fashion are defined in contrast to it.

definition.text: Turning waste or unwanted products into new materials or products seen as having greater quality or value, such as artistic or environmental value.

facts.text: It is a subset of recycling that adds value, unlike downcycling, which turns waste into lower-quality products.
Before the Industrial Revolution, upcycling to repair goods was common; mass production and a linear model of throwing things away reduced it.
The terms upcycling and downcycling first appeared in print in a 1994 SalvoNEWS article.
It is a circular economy strategy that cuts resource use by raising product value and extending product lifespans through repair and repurposing.
In poorer countries it reflects a lack of access to new goods; in rich countries, more concern for the environment.

definition.text: Recovering rare metals from a society's stockpile of discarded electronic waste, its 'urban mine', by mechanical and chemical treatment.

facts.text: A 2010 Japanese government study estimated 6,800 tonnes of gold could be recovered from used electronics in Japan.
Its main aim is recovering materials, whereas landfill mining aims to fix problems at the disposal site.
In developing countries e-waste is often recycled informally, even inside homes, without proper equipment.
Shifting from primary production to urban mining needs detailed accounts of materials in use and in obsolete stocks.

definition.text: Giving economic value to waste or residues by reusing or recycling them into useful materials.

facts.text: It usually means using the residue of one industrial process as raw material or energy for another.
Industrial wastes suit it best because they are more consistent and predictable than household waste.
Interest grew with tighter regulation of residues and the spread of sustainable development and circular economy ideas in the 1990s and 2000s.
Mine tailings, red mud from alumina production, and even spent nuclear fuel can be valorised.

definition.text: Turning food waste into food or feed products, or extracting food or feed ingredients from it.

facts.text: Landfilled food waste releases methane and other harmful compounds.
Food wastes can yield biofertilisers, bioplastics, biofuels, chemicals and nutraceuticals, and can be converted into insect protein.
About 30% of the food livestock eat comes from food waste or crops grown and processed in the supply chain.

definition.text: A set of principles focused on preventing waste by redesigning how resources flow so that all products are reused or repurposed.

facts.text: Its goal is to send nothing to landfills, incinerators, oceans or anywhere else in the environment.
It aims to prevent waste rather than manage it at the end of the pipe, as a 'whole systems' change in how materials flow through society.
Currently 9% of global plastic is recycled.
Reaching it requires products that are easy to take apart for recycling, plus durability, repairability and minimal packaging.
Bea Johnson's '5 Rs' (refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle, rot) extend the 3 Rs for households.
Many organisations and cities adopt the zero waste slogan without pressing for its key changes.

definition.text: A ranking of policies and strategies for a zero-waste system, from the highest and best use of materials to the lowest.

facts.text: It adds depth to the 3Rs and encourages policy and investment at the top of the hierarchy.
It is meant for everyone from policymakers to industry and individuals, and helps evaluate proposed solutions.
